text: Chapter one. What We're Building. The same system, zero code, free tools only.

Here's the thing. You don't need our website to trade like we do. Everything the Market Watch scanner does, regime detection, multi-strategy screening, scoring, position tracking, you can replicate all of it with free tools you already have access to. Finviz for screening. Google Sheets for tracking. Yahoo Finance or Webull for alerts. Same results, zero programming, about fifteen minutes a day. Let me show you exactly how.

Let's compare the two systems side by side. Our Market Watch scanner runs automatically every night at ten thirty. It pre-screens a hundred and sixteen tickers, uses a four-factor composite scoring system, runs three backtested portfolio modes, and sends alerts via Telegram and YouTube. Your D-I-Y version? You do it manually in fifteen minutes each evening. You use the same tickers via Finviz presets. You apply a simplified three-factor scoring. You track one portfolio mode in Google Sheets. And you set price alerts on Yahoo or Webull. The core logic is identical. The difference is automation versus your fifteen minutes of effort.

Here's your complete toolkit, and everything is free. First, Finviz dot com. It's a free stock screener with R-S-I, volume, moving averages, A-T-R, and sector filters. No account needed. Second, Google Sheets. This will be your portfolio tracker, position log, and scoring sheet. I'll give you the template. Third, Yahoo Finance or Webull for price alerts on stop losses, T-P-1, T-P-2, and timeout reminders. Fourth, TradingView's free tier is optional but useful for charts with indicators for visual confirmation. And fifth, a thirty-second VIX check. Just Google VIX index to determine your market regime before screening.

Quiz time. How much does it cost to replicate the Market Watch scanner system manually? Is it A, ninety-nine dollars a month for premium tools? B, zero dollars because everything uses free tiers? C, twenty-nine dollars a month for Finviz Elite? Or D, you need Bloomberg Terminal access? The answer is B. Zero dollars. Every single tool in this system is completely free. Finviz free tier, Google Sheets, Yahoo Finance, TradingView free plan. You only invest your time, about fifteen minutes per evening.
Chapter two. Step one, check market regime. Thirty seconds to know what kind of market you're in.

This is the most important step and most people skip it. The VIX tells you what kind of market you're in. Below eighteen? That's Risk-On. Screen for momentum breakouts in growth sectors. Eighteen to twenty-two? Neutral. Run a mix of all strategies equally. Twenty-two to twenty-eight? Early Risk-Off. Focus on pullbacks in defensive and energy stocks. Above twenty-eight? Full Risk-Off. Only look for oversold bounces in quality names. You can find the current VIX in three seconds by just Googling it.

Here's the thirty-second regime check. Step one, Google VIX index. The current value appears instantly at the top of the results. Below eighteen means green light. Above twenty-eight means red alert. Step two, check the S and P five hundred trend. Is S-P-Y above or below its fifty-day moving average? Above means bullish, below means bearish. Step three, note the regime at the top of today's screening notes. This determines which Finviz preset you'll run next.

Why does regime matter so much? In Risk-On, you run the Momentum and Breakout screeners. In Risk-Off, you ONLY run the Oversold Bounce screener targeting defensive sectors. In Neutral, you run all three. Skipping this step is the number one reason D-I-Y screeners fail. They run momentum screens in a crash and get absolutely destroyed. Don't be that person.
Chapter three. Strategy one, Oversold Bounce. Finding beaten-down stocks that are ready to snap back.

The oversold bounce is probably the most intuitive strategy. When a quality stock gets hammered and its R-S-I drops below thirty-five, it's statistically likely to bounce. We add a volume filter because high volume on the drop means institutions are stepping in, not just retail panic selling. And we add a market cap floor to avoid penny stocks. Put it all together and you have a reliable mean-reversion setup that works in any market regime.

Let me walk you through the exact Finviz setup. Go to finviz dot com slash screener dot ashx. Click the Technical tab at the top. Set R-S-I fourteen to Oversold, which is below thirty. Or select Under forty if you want more results. Set Relative Volume to Over one point five. This ensures volume is at least fifty percent above normal, meaning institutions are trading. Set Market Cap to Mid, which is two billion to ten billion, or Large, which is over ten billion. No micro-caps. Set Average Volume to Over five hundred K for liquidity. Then click Charts view and scan visually. Look for a clear drop followed by a volume spike. That's your signal.

Here's the filter summary in table form. R-S-I fourteen set to Oversold or Under forty because the stock is beaten down and a bounce is likely. Relative Volume over one point five because unusual activity means institutional interest. Market Cap Mid or Large, over two billion dollars, to avoid junk and focus on quality bounces. Average Volume over five hundred thousand for enough liquidity to enter and exit. Country set to U-S-A for best data coverage. And optionally, you can filter by sector, choosing Energy, Healthcare, or Industrials, which are defensive sectors that work better in Risk-Off environments.

Pro tip. Finviz saves your filter configuration in the browser address bar as a URL. So bookmark each strategy as a separate bookmark. Tomorrow, just click the bookmark and the exact same filters load instantly. Label them M-W Oversold, M-W Momentum, and M-W Breakout. Three clicks, three screens, done in five minutes. This tiny optimization saves you from re-entering filters every single day.

Quiz. You run the Oversold Bounce screener and find a stock with R-S-I twenty-five, relative volume three point two, but market cap is only one hundred and eighty million dollars. Should you trade it? A, yes, the R-S-I and volume are perfect? B, no, market cap is too small, high manipulation risk? C, yes, small caps have bigger bounces? Or D, maybe, check the news first? The answer is B. A one hundred and eighty million dollar market cap stock is a micro-cap. These are easily manipulated, have poor liquidity, and are often targets of pump-and-dump schemes. Always stick to the two billion dollar plus market cap filter. Quality over excitement.
Chapter four. Strategy two, Momentum Expansion. Riding stocks that are already moving up, with volume proof.

Momentum trading means buying strength, not weakness. A stock trading above its twenty-day moving average with double its normal volume is sending a clear signal. Big money is coming in. The R-S-I between fifty and seventy-five confirms the move has room to run. It's strong but not yet overbought. This is the bread-and-butter strategy in Risk-On markets. When the VIX is below eighteen and everything is green, this is where you make your money.

Here's the Finviz setup for Momentum. In the Technical tab, set twenty-day Simple Moving Average to Price above S-M-A twenty. This confirms the stock is in an uptrend. Set Relative Volume to Over two. Double normal volume is the expansion part, it means money is flooding in. Set R-S-I fourteen to Not Overbought, which gives you the fifty to seventy sweet spot. Strong enough to confirm momentum, not so high it's about to reverse. Market Cap stays Mid or Large. In the Descriptive tab, set Change to Up so you only see stocks that are green today. Finally, sort by Relative Volume descending. The highest volume surge stocks appear first, those have the strongest momentum signal.

The momentum filter summary. Twenty-day S-M-A set to Price above S-M-A twenty confirms the short-term uptrend. Relative Volume over two means double normal volume, which equals institutional buying. R-S-I fourteen Not Overbought keeps you in the fifty to seventy range with room to run before exhaustion. Market Cap Mid or Large for quality and liquidity. Change set to Up so you only see green stocks today. And Average Volume over five hundred K so you can enter and exit without slippage.

Important warning. When NOT to run momentum screens. If the VIX is above twenty-eight and the S and P five hundred is below its fifty-day moving average, do NOT run this screener. Momentum strategies in Risk-Off markets produce false signals constantly. Everything looks like a bounce until it drops another five percent. Save this strategy for green regimes only. This is why we check the VIX first, every single day.
Chapter five. Strategy three, Breakout Squeeze. Catching stocks exploding through resistance with expanding volatility.

A breakout happens when a stock that's been consolidating near resistance finally pushes through with conviction. The key confirmation is expanding volatility, measured by A-T-R, combined with the price clearing the fifty-day moving average. In Finviz terms, you're looking for new highs on high volume above a key moving average. This is the most exciting strategy but also requires the most discipline, because fake breakouts are common.

The Finviz setup for Breakout. First, set fifty-day S-M-A to Price above S-M-A fifty. This confirms the stock is in a medium-term uptrend, not just a dead-cat bounce. Second, in the Technical tab, select New High. The stock is breaking out right now. Third, set Relative Volume to Over one point five. A breakout on low volume is a fake-out. High volume confirms institutional participation. Fourth, set weekly volatility to Over three percent. This is the squeeze part. Volatility is expanding, which means the move has energy. Fifth, Market Cap can be Small, three hundred million to two billion, or Mid and Large. Breakouts work across all cap sizes. And sixth, always review charts manually. Look for a clear consolidation pattern, like a flag, triangle, or range, that just broke. That's your entry.

Breakout filter summary. Fifty-day S-M-A confirms the medium-term uptrend. New High means the stock is breaking out now. Relative Volume over one point five confirms the breakout is real with institutional participation. Weekly Volatility over three percent shows the squeeze is releasing. Market Cap Small plus, above three hundred million, gives you flexibility but still avoids micro-caps. And Average Volume over three hundred K ensures enough liquidity for clean execution.

Bonus trick. In the Finviz screener results, click the T-A view, which stands for Technical Analysis. Finviz shows you the chart with all indicators overlaid. S-M-A lines, volume bars, R-S-I, everything on one screen. You can visually confirm the breakout pattern in three seconds without opening another tool. If the chart looks messy or the breakout is weak, skip it. Clean charts make clean trades.

Quiz. A stock is at a new fifty-two week high with relative volume of zero point six, which is below average. Is this a valid breakout? A, yes, new highs are always bullish? B, no, low volume breakouts are unreliable and often reverse? C, yes, volume doesn't matter for breakouts? Or D, maybe, wait for volume to pick up tomorrow? The answer is B. A breakout on low volume is one of the most common false signals in trading. Without institutional participation, which is that volume surge, the breakout lacks conviction and frequently reverses within days. Always require relative volume above one point five for breakout trades.
Chapter six. Scoring and Selection. How to pick your Top five from the screener results, manually, in about ten minutes.

Our automated scanner uses four factors with complex weighting. For your manual version, we simplify to three factors you can evaluate in sixty seconds per stock. Technical setup quality, volume confirmation, and chart clarity. Each factor is scored one to three. Total score ranges from three to nine. The rule is simple. Only trade setups scoring seven or above. Everything below seven lacks sufficient confluence and has a significantly lower success rate.

Here's the scoring sheet. Three factors, each scored one to three points. Factor one is Technical Setup. Score one if R-S-I is borderline and price barely above a moving average. Score two if R-S-I gives a clear signal and price is above one M-A. Score three if R-S-I is in the perfect zone and price is above both S-M-A twenty and fifty. Factor two is Volume. Score one for relative volume between one point five and two X. Score two for two to three X. Score three for three X plus, which is massive institutional activity. Factor three is Chart Clarity. Score one if the chart is messy with no clear pattern. Score two for a decent pattern with some noise. Score three for a clean, textbook setup. Add them up. Seven or above? That's a trade.

The selection process takes about ten minutes. Step one, run all three screeners. Open your three bookmarked Finviz URLs. Takes thirty seconds. Step two, collect candidates. Note every stock that appears. Typically you'll get ten to thirty results across all three screens. Step three, quick chart check. Open the Finviz chart for each. Spend fifteen seconds per chart. Eliminate ugly charts immediately. Step four, score the survivors. Apply the three-factor scoring to remaining candidates. Takes about one minute per stock. Step five, pick your Top five. Sort by total score. Take the top five that score seven or above. These are your signals for tomorrow.

This next step is absolutely non-negotiable. The dilution check. It takes thirty seconds per stock but it can save your entire account. For EVERY stock in your Top five, do a quick Google search. Type the ticker plus the word dilution or offering. If you see any mention of an A-T-M offering, warrants, shelf registration, or a recent S-3 filing in the last ninety days, remove it from your list immediately. No exceptions. This thirty-second check saved us from the INDO disaster where a technically perfect setup got crushed by a surprise dilution. The chart looked amazing. The fundamentals looked fine. But the S-E-C filings showed warrants and toxic financing that were invisible on the price chart.

Now let's set your levels. Entry price is the previous day's close or a limit order within one percent. Stop Loss goes below the nearest support level, typically six to eight percent below entry. Target one is where you sell fifty percent of your position, usually at the next resistance level or ten to fifteen percent above entry. Target two is where you sell the rest, calculated as two times the distance to your stop loss. The minimum risk-to-reward ratio should be one point five to one or better. If the math doesn't work, skip the trade. And finally, set a timeout of five trading days. If no exit has been hit after five days, close the position at market price regardless.

Quiz. Your screener returns twenty results. After chart review and scoring, three stocks score eight out of nine and seven stocks score five to six out of nine. How many do you trade? A, all ten because diversification is key? B, only the three scoring eight or above because quality beats quantity? C, the top seven because anything above five is tradeable? Or D, none because you should wait for a day with more nine out of nine scores? The answer is B. Only trade setups scoring seven or above. The three stocks scoring eight are your A-grade picks. The five to six scores lack sufficient confluence and have a much lower success rate. Patience and selectivity are your edge.
Chapter seven. Your Google Sheets Tracker. Position management, exits, and performance tracking, all in one simple spreadsheet.

Here are the columns for your Google Sheets portfolio tracker. Column A is Date, the scan date. Column B is Ticker, the stock symbol. Column C is Strategy, which screen found it. Column D is Score, your three-factor score from three to nine. Column E is Entry, your entry price. Column F is Stop, your stop loss price. Column G is T-P-1, your first target where you sell fifty percent. Column H is T-P-2, your second target where you sell the rest. Column I is Timeout, the date to force-close, which is five trading days after entry. Column J is Status. Open, T-P-1 hit, T-P-2 hit, stopped out, or expired. Column K is Exit Price. And Column L is P and L percent, calculated as exit price minus entry divided by entry. Simple, complete, and everything you need to track your performance.

Setting up price alerts is free and takes two minutes. Option one, Yahoo Finance app. Search the ticker, tap the bell icon, and set price alerts at your Stop Loss and T-P-1 prices. You get a push notification on your phone. Option two, Webull app. Search the ticker, go to Price Alert, and set upper and lower thresholds. Instant notification. Option three, TradingView free tier. On any chart, right-click the price axis, click Add Alert, and set your conditions. The free tier allows two active alerts. And finally, set a calendar reminder on your phone for the timeout date, five trading days after entry. If no alert has fired by then, check and close the position.

Position sizing. Here's the simple rule that most beginners overthink. Decide how many slots you want. We recommend four for most people. Divide your trading capital by four. That's your position size. Period. If you have ten thousand dollars, each trade gets twenty-five hundred. When a position closes, the cash returns to the pool. When you open a new position, use the same fixed amount. Don't increase size after a win. Don't decrease after a loss. Consistency is the entire game. The professionals who survive decades in this business all use fixed position sizing. It's boring. It works.

Your daily routine. Fifteen minutes total. At six PM, check the VIX. Thirty seconds. Google VIX, note the regime, and that tells you which screeners to run. At six oh one, run your Finviz screens. Five minutes. Click your three bookmarks, or only one or two based on regime, and scan the results. At six oh six, score and select. Five minutes. Chart-check each candidate, score them, pick your top three to five, and do the thirty-second dilution check on each. At six eleven, update your spreadsheet. Three minutes. Add new signals, update open positions, mark any exits from today's alerts. At six fourteen, set alerts. Two minutes. Yahoo or Webull alerts for new entries, stop loss and T-P-1 prices. And then you're done. Live your life. The alerts will notify you when action is needed. No screen-watching required.

Exit rules cheat sheet. When to act. Stop loss alert fires? Sell immediately, no debate, no hoping, no praying. T-P-1 alert fires? Sell fifty percent and move your stop to breakeven. You now have a free trade. T-P-2 alert fires? Sell the remaining fifty percent. Job done. Timeout at day five? Close at market price, whatever it is. No extensions. Now, when to do nothing. Price moving sideways? Let it play out, that's why you have a timeout. Down three percent but stop not hit? Trust your stop level. News is scary but the stock is fine? Ignore the noise. A friend says sell? Follow your system, not opinions.

You might be wondering, when will my results start matching the Market Watch scanner? After about ten trading days of following this system consistently, your results will start to converge. Why? Because you're using the same core logic. Regime-aware screening. Volume-confirmed entries. Mechanical exits. And fixed position sizing. The automated version is faster and covers more tickers, but the edge comes from the PROCESS, not the technology. The algorithm doesn't have a secret sauce. It just follows these exact rules without emotion, every single day.

Based on backtesting, here's what you can expect. Win rate between forty-five and fifty-five percent. That means about half your trades will lose. And that's completely fine. Average win of eight to twelve percent. Average loss of five to seven percent. Notice how the average win is bigger than the average loss. That's the edge. And your expected monthly return? Two to five percent. Not spectacular, but compounded over a year, that's twenty-five to eighty percent. Consistently. Without gambling.

Let's recap your complete D-I-Y scanner checklist. Check VIX daily for market regime, thirty seconds. Bookmark three Finviz screener presets for Oversold, Momentum, and Breakout. Run regime-appropriate screens each evening, five minutes. Score results with the three-factor system, pick Top five scoring seven or above. Quick dilution check, Google ticker plus dilution for each pick. Log everything in Google Sheets, date, entry, stop, T-P-1, T-P-2, timeout. Set Yahoo or Webull alerts for stop loss and T-P-1 on every position. Position size equals total capital divided by four slots, fixed amount each trade. At T-P-1, sell fifty percent and trail stop to breakeven. At timeout day five, close regardless of P and L. Review your spreadsheet weekly and calculate win rate and profit factor. And the golden rule: never cherry-pick, never skip stops, follow the system.

And here's the secret that nobody talks about. It's not the tool. It's the process. Professional traders don't win because they have better software. They win because they have a process they follow every single day without exception. You now have that process. Three screeners. A scoring sheet. A spreadsheet tracker. And ironclad exit rules. Fifteen minutes a day. Zero cost. Same edge. The rest? That's discipline. And discipline is a muscle. The more you use it, the stronger it gets. Go build your system. Start tonight.

Final quiz. What is the single biggest advantage of building your own D-I-Y scanner versus using a paid signal service? A, it's cheaper? B, you understand WHY every trade is taken, building real trading skill? C, you get more signals? Or D, the signals are better quality? The answer is B. The biggest advantage isn't the cost savings, it's the education. When you build and run the screens yourself, you understand the logic behind every trade. If a trade fails, you know why. If the market changes, you can adapt. A paid signal service keeps you dependent. Your D-I-Y system makes you independent. And that independence? That's the real edge. Thanks for watching. Now go build your scanner.
